statement: Saffire flies on uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft after they leave the station, so fires larger than is safe near a crew can be tested.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: Saffire stays dormant while the cargo ship is docked, is started by ground command after the ship moves to a separate orbit, and sends its data down before reentry.
source_title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety (NTRS 20180005168, abstract)

statement: NASA reports that, in the Saffire experiments, reducing pressure slows flame spread.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)
caveat: Stated as a summary finding; the page gives no numbers.

statement: Saffire-I test 1-1 (SIBAL fabric, 20 cm/s concurrent flow, oxygen about 21.7 to 21.5 percent) burned for 420 s at about 1.8 mm/s, with about 84 cm of fabric consumed.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)
caveat: Pressure is not stated in the source.

statement: Saffire-I test 1-2 (same fabric and flow speed, opposed flow, oxygen about 21.5 percent) burned for 70 s at about 1.3 mm/s, with about 10 cm consumed.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)
caveat: Pressure is not stated in the source.

statement: In Saffire-I the concurrent-flow flame stabilized at a length of about 40 mm in the plateau stage, versus about 24 mm for the opposed-flow flame.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)

statement: In Saffire-II, silicone samples of three thicknesses did not sustain flame spread in microgravity at 20 cm/s, although some of them burned in normal gravity.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)
caveat: Samples 2-1 and 2-4 were almost fully consumed in 1 g; 2-3 did not burn in either condition.

statement: In Saffire-II, cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full 29 cm length: 145 s at 20 cm/s and 115 s at 25 cm/s, with spread rates of about 2.1 and 2.6 mm/s.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)

statement: In Saffire-II, thick PMMA slabs burned for 600 s and 900 s with only about 10 cm of visible damage, the flame staying anchored near the base.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)

statement: Saffire-III repeats the Saffire-I setup at a different flow speed, planned in pre-flight slides at close to 30 cm/s instead of 20 cm/s, and uses the same fabric (75 percent cotton, 25 percent fiberglass).
source_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (NTRS 20170002628)
caveat: Pre-flight planning statement from 2017 slides. No Saffire-III results appear in that document.

statement: A 2024 summary says the first Saffire flights showed that fires can grow large, that average temperature and pressure rise was not the main worry, and that rising CO and CO2 raised health concerns.
source_title: Saffire VI paper, ICES 2024 (NTRS 20240002981)
caveat: Summarised by the Saffire VI paper from earlier references.

statement: The Saffire abstract states that flame growth reached a steady size in some tests and that enclosure size affected flame spread more than expected.
source_title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety (NTRS 20180005168, abstract)

statement: In Saffire VI, with the smoke alarm threshold set at 1 mg per cubic metre (described as relatively tight), the FFD detector reached it at 981 s, by which time much of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
source_title: Saffire VI paper, ICES 2024 (NTRS 20240002981)
caveat: Wording confirmed by a second reading. Which Saffire VI test this refers to was not confirmed.

statement: In Saffire VI, both PMMA tests exceeded the allowable 1-hour CO2 partial pressure of 3 mmHg. The paper gives CO limits of 425 ppm (1-hour) and 100 ppm (24-hour), and Table 2 lists CO increases of 308 and 320 ppm for the two PMMA tests.
source_title: Saffire VI paper, ICES 2024 (NTRS 20240002981)
caveat: CO2 exceedance is quoted from the paper. CO increases come from Table 2, whose column mapping is uncertain, and the paper's wording on CO versus its limits was not confirmed.

statement: The Saffire VI paper states that further work is needed to extend its results to the partial-gravity environment expected on future Moon and Mars missions.
source_title: Saffire VI paper, ICES 2024 (NTRS 20240002981)
caveat: Wording confirmed by a second reading.

statement: SAME measured the size distribution of smoke from Teflon, Kapton, cellulose, silicone rubber and a wick-fed liquid, as sample temperature, airflow and smoke age changed.
source_title: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

statement: SAME-R reflew during Expedition 24 (July to September 2010) with Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell, adding electron microscopy of collected particles.
source_title: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

statement: Mean smoke particle diameters were roughly 100 to 200 nm, but a large share of particle mass sat above 1 micrometre (about half for silicone rubber, whose mean diameter was 227 nm).
source_title: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

statement: As smoke aged, particle counts dropped sharply while total mass stayed fairly steady, consistent with particles merging.
source_title: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

statement: Space Shuttle smoke detectors used ionization and screened out particles above about 1 to 2 micrometres; ISS detectors use near-infrared forward light scattering and respond best to particles above 1 micrometre.
source_title: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

statement: NASA's SAME summary concludes that all samples made many sub-micron particles that ionization detectors sense well, and that a light-scattering detector would work very well in most cases.
source_title: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
caveat: The page gives no detector thresholds or measured detector performance.

statement: NASA describes BASS as one of the first investigations of putting out fires in microgravity, noting that ground methods could be ineffective or even worsen a flame.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: NASA says space firefighting has to account for flame geometry, the material, and the extinguishing method.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: BASS-II burned acrylic films, sheets and rods, a cotton-fiberglass fabric, and a large acrylic sphere in a small flow duct inside the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox.
source_title: NASA Glenn: BASS-II project page

statement: In BASS-II the duct airflow was varied from 5 to 50 cm/s and oxygen was varied by diluting the glovebox volume with nitrogen; pressure is not listed as a variable.
source_title: NASA Glenn: BASS-II project page

statement: BASS-II determined spread rates for thin and thick fuels and a formula for the transition between them, and found that models predicted higher spread rates than were observed.
source_title: NASA Glenn: BASS-II project page

statement: BASS-II heat release was mostly well under 100 W, and the average global fuel-to-oxygen equivalence ratio was about 1.3 (fuel-rich).
source_title: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (abstract)

statement: BASS-II was the first ISS test to dilute the glovebox working volume with nitrogen, using a stirred-reactor model to set the nitrogen flow.
source_title: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (abstract)

statement: NASA's Glenn page says 41 test samples would be burned for 89 test points in BASS-II.
source_title: NASA Glenn: BASS-II project page
caveat: Phrased as a plan on the page; final counts may differ.

statement: FLEX tested how well fire suppressants work and led to the discovery of cool flames, which can keep burning after the visible flame is gone.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: FLEX-2 studied how quickly fuel droplets burn, when soot forms, and how liquid fuel mixtures evaporate before burning.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: Analysis of 59 Burning Rate Emulator tests covered heat flow, flame size and fuel mixture flow; NASA says it may show whether current flammability tests work in microgravity.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: SoFIE-GEL burned solid spherical samples and found that observations agreed with model trends for how fuel temperature affects flammability.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: The Confined Combustion study found that confinement affects fire hazard and, depending on conditions, can raise or lower the flammability of solid fuels.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: FLARE, a JAXA experiment, tests materials flammability in microgravity to improve fire safety on future missions.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)
caveat: NASA's FLARE project page describes it as an international project (JAXA, NASA, ESA and others); see F47.

statement: NASA notes that without buoyancy, low-momentum flames in microgravity tend to be rounded or spherical.
source_title: NASA: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety (Dec 2023, updated Mar 2024)

statement: The PSI database holds raw and processed data plus documentation, models, images and publications for each catalogued study.
source_title: NASA PSI spotlight

statement: NASA's PSI research call asks for new analyses of existing PSI data, including with artificial intelligence or machine learning.
source_title: NASA ROSES: Physical Sciences Informatics research opportunity

statement: In Saffire-II, most samples were ignited with an 80 W heater for 9.2 s, and the two thick PMMA slabs with 97 W for 30 s.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (NTRS 20170008805)
caveat: Saffire-II values. Igniter durations for Saffire-I and III were not found in the sources read, so this is only a plausibility guide.

statement: SPICE investigated the transition from non-sooting to sooting flames, aiming at simple predictions of soot emissions, and ran in 2009 in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox.
source_title: NASA: Combustion in Reduced Gravity on the ISS (booklet NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
caveat: Automated reading of the booklet PDF.

statement: SLICE used the SPICE hardware to study lifted and lifting flames in the glovebox, started and completed operations in 2012, and is described as a precursor to the CLD Flame experiment.
source_title: NASA: Combustion in Reduced Gravity on the ISS (booklet NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
caveat: Automated reading of the booklet PDF. No findings are reported there.

statement: NASA's booklet describes DAFT as examining background aerosol particulate levels on the ISS and states no results.
source_title: NASA: Combustion in Reduced Gravity on the ISS (booklet NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
caveat: The booklet spells the name 'Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test' and does not use the DAFT acronym.

statement: ACME is described as five experiments for the Combustion Integrated Rack (BRE, CLD Flame, E-FIELD Flames, Flame Design, s-Flame), focused on soot processes, flame stability and extinction, materials flammability and electric-field effects.
source_title: NASA: Combustion in Reduced Gravity on the ISS (booklet NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
caveat: Pre-flight description (operations were then expected to begin in 2016). No results are stated.

statement: NASA's booklet reports that recent BASS results indicate the standard NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 flammability screening is not conservative, and that materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
source_title: NASA: Combustion in Reduced Gravity on the ISS (booklet NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
caveat: Automated reading of the booklet PDF. The figures behind the statement are not given there, and the matching limit rows in the Evidence Lab are unconfirmed.

statement: NASA's SoFIE page says the NASA-STD-6001 flammability requirements use a 1-g flame-spread test that some researchers believe is not conservative in low gravity, and presents SoFIE microgravity tests as one way to examine that concern.
source_title: NASA Glenn: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE)
caveat: The page reports no SoFIE results, so it does not say whether the 1-g test is conservative.

statement: FM2 is described by NASA as the first combustion experiment on another planetary body; modeling plus parabolic-flight and ISS work suggest materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity than on Earth.
source_title: NASA Glenn: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)
caveat: Planned experiment: the page gives no oxygen or pressure values, schedule or results. The suggestion about lower oxygen is from modeling and earlier tests, not from FM2.

statement: NASA's FLARE page says the project aims to correlate material flammability limits in normal gravity and microgravity, so limits in microgravity can be estimated from ground data, and to give a new spacecraft-material screening test that addresses shortcomings of NASA STD 6001B.
source_title: NASA Glenn: Flammability Limits at Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE)
caveat: Method goal only: no numeric limits are given, and the page's flight date ('2017 or later') is outdated.

statement: The BASS-II test matrix supplied with this project lists 129 tests across six investigator sheets, with calibrated initial oxygen from 13.6 to 22.2 percent by volume and initial and final CO2 and CO readings where recorded.
source_title: BASS-II Test Matrix by PI (xlsx supplied by the author)
caveat: Fan and air settings are instrument display readings, not cm/s. Final CO is missing for 9 tests. The author states the file comes from PSI (PSI-25); that is not confirmed here. The page linked here is the BASS-II project page, not the file.

statement: The FLEX test plan quotes an earlier study of methane cup-burner flames (Takahashi et al., 2004) in which the minimum extinction concentration of CO2 is 0.16 in normal gravity and 0.19 in microgravity, of helium 0.27 and 0.31, and of nitrogen 0.26 and 0.38.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan (PDF supplied by the author; extracted from the FLEX Research Requirements Document, 4 Nov 2005)
caveat: Quoted from a cup-burner study of gas flames, not a FLEX droplet result, and the plan describes the microgravity values as simulations. The link is PSI's search page because the file has no direct link.

statement: The FLEX test plan describes finding the limiting oxygen index, the lowest oxygen concentration that supports a quasi-steady flame, as a function of ambient pressure between 0.5 and 1.5 atm, starting with droplets of about 3 mm.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan (PDF supplied by the author; extracted from the FLEX Research Requirements Document, 4 Nov 2005)
caveat: A planning document, not results: the pressures and droplet sizes are planned conditions. The link is PSI's search page because the file has no direct link.

statement: The FLEX test plan defines the limiting oxygen index (LOI) as the lowest oxygen concentration that can support a quasi-steady flame for a given material and ambient condition, and says that for fire safety the aim of a total-flooding agent is to bring oxygen below the LOI.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan (extract of the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity, 4 Nov 2005); file supplied by the author
caveat: The LOI depends on the fuel, pressure, diluent and geometry, so it is not one universal threshold. The PDF was supplied by the author and its PSI origin is not confirmed.

statement: The FLEX test plan reports that Katta et al. (2004) found a CO2 volume fraction above 19.1 percent was needed to destabilize a methane-air flame base in microgravity, compared with 16.4 percent in normal gravity.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan (extract of the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity, 4 Nov 2005); file supplied by the author
caveat: A methane cup-burner flame, quoted second-hand from a 2004 study. It does not show what CO2 level would suppress a spacecraft material fire. The PDF was supplied by the author and its PSI origin is not confirmed.
